failures.rule: a substitution that resolves to an object means an object for concatenation, and concatenating an object with an array is an error
a substitution that resolves to an array means an array for concatenation, and concatenating an array with an object is an error

an object whose field a is itself a merge of an object and a substitution concatenates with a substituted object like any other: the two merge. typesafe/config fails with an internal error (BugOrBroken) because the concatenation is not registered as the merge's parent; the same objects written as literals concatenate fine

${a} in a's own value refers to the earlier a, an object, so the concatenation merges {p: ...} with {q: 1}; the inner p is itself a merge of an object and a substitution. typesafe/config fails with an internal error (BugOrBroken) when the merge inside a concatenation piece resolves, as in 018
${tail} is a list, so it concatenates with the list before it, whose object keeps foo = 1 under the undefined ${?bar}; typesafe/config fails with an internal error (lightbend/config#751)

${x} is x's object {q:2}; the 5 it overrode is x's history, not its value, so { p = 1 } ${x} merges into {p:1, q:2}. The rule of duplicate-keys-and-object-merging/029 reached through concatenation instead of a duplicate key; typesafe/config 1.4.9 lets the 5 cut the merge and keeps only {q:2}
the implicit root object follows the object comma rules, so its last field may carry a single trailing comma
between substitutions that resolve to objects, unquoted whitespace is ignored but quoted whitespace should be an error
unquoted whitespace between substitutions that resolve to objects or lists must be ignored, so they merge and concatenate as if adjacent
whitespace between two list substitutions is ignored, tabs included, and the lists concatenate
U+00A0 is a Zs space and so whitespace in HOCON; between two list substitutions it is ignored (lightbend/config#862 review)
the BOM must be treated as whitespace, so between two list substitutions it is ignored
an undefined optional substitution in a concatenation with an array becomes an empty array

the mirror of 008: an undefined optional substitution before an array becomes an empty array too. typesafe/config keeps the whitespace before the list as text and rejects it, while accepting 008 (noted on lightbend/config#862)

the object twin of 009: an undefined optional substitution before an object substitution becomes an empty object and the whitespace between them is ignored. typesafe/config keeps the whitespace before the object as text and rejects it, while accepting ${x} ${?absent}

the null at r only stops merging at r; ${r} is the object {x:1}, and a later object merges with the earlier a, so helper stays. typesafe/config carries r's null through the substitution and drops helper (lightbend/config#864)
the same rule one level down: the null in v.nested's history belongs to v.nested, so a.nested still merges with the substituted {x:1} (lightbend/config#864)

a substitution sees the resolved value of the field it names, so o24bbd equals a.nested, which keeps helper. The key name is chosen to sort before a in typesafe/config's root HashMap, the order in which the first version of lightbend/config#864 answered differently for the two
the null belongs to v's history even when v's object is still unresolved, so a merges and keeps helper (lightbend/config#864)

${r} is an object, so it merges with the earlier a and the ${missing} inside it is evaluated: an error. typesafe/config 1.4.5 agreed; 1.4.9 drops the earlier a and yields {y:1}, and lightbend/config#864 restores the error

v's value is a merge whose top is an object and whose null sits further down, under nested; that null is still v.nested's merge instruction, so a.nested keeps helper (lightbend/config#864 review, round 3)
two objects merge, so the empty later object keeps x; replacement would have given {}
four values for a, two of them substitutions that resolve to objects: all four merge in order
the object layer of a's merge contains a field b that is itself a merge of a substitution and an object; both levels merge
the same shape with a key the object does not have: the list below it is not consulted, a.b is undefined and the optional p is not created
null is a non-object value, so the second object's null is used for b rather than dropped

${x} is x's merged object {q:2}; the 5 below it is x's history, not a's, so a's two objects merge into {p:1, q:2}. The same rule as 010–017 with a scalar instead of null; typesafe/config 1.4.9 lets the 5 cut a's merge

a file named .json is in JSON format, and an unquoted value is not JSON. typesafe/config parses a .json named outright with the HOCON parser, so the file is accepted; the same file found through a basename is rejected

in a properties file a dotted key is a path, so a.b and a.c build an object at a; the spec's Java properties mapping says the object must always win when a key is both a value and a parent, whatever the order; values are strings
the .json file is found through a basename, so it is parsed as JSON; an unquoted value is a HOCON extension, not JSON
the .json file is found through a basename, so it is parsed as JSON; JSON has no trailing commas
the .json file is found through a basename, so it is parsed as JSON; the spec's own footing is that duplicate keys are invalid JSON (L194-195), so the second a is an error rather than an override
the .json file is found through a basename, so it is parsed as JSON; JSON separates array elements with commas only; whitespace does not concatenate or separate
the .json file is found through a basename, so it is parsed as JSON; an empty document is not JSON, although it is an empty HOCON object
the .json file is found through a basename, so it is parsed as JSON; a JSON key is a quoted string; a number cannot be a key
the .json file is found through a basename, so it is parsed as JSON; in JSON a newline between fields does not stand in for the comma
the .json file is found through a basename, so it is parsed as JSON; JSON forbids a leading zero on a number. typesafe/config reads 01 as 1, the same leniency it shows in HOCON
for a URL, file: included, only the exact URL is used and no extension is tried: inc does not exist, though inc.conf beside it does, so the include finds nothing and, not required, adds nothing
the .json file is found through a basename, so it is parsed as JSON; // and # comments are a HOCON extension, and JSON has none
the .json file is found through a basename, so it is parsed as JSON; a JSON string may not hold a raw control character, and a tab is one, so it must be written as \t

the .json file is found through a basename, so it is parsed as JSON; JSON whitespace is only space, tab, LF and CR, and the wider set with the no-break space 0x00A0 is defined for HOCON only (L167-172). typesafe/config treats a no-break space as whitespace in JSON too
an absolute path is loaded as such, so the file of the same name beside main.conf is not it; the absolute file does not exist and the include is ignored
a file() argument is not interpreted relative to the including file, so the marker beside sub/inner.conf is not loaded; nothing of that name exists elsewhere and the include is ignored
the included file may contain substitutions like any other; typesafe/config refuses an include nested in a list when the included file is not fully resolved
the included file leaves a as an object merged with a substitution; that whole stack merges with the object the including file set earlier
the earlier value is itself a substitution; once everything resolves to objects, all three layers merge
the earlier value is a number, so the included object stack replaces it and merges only within itself
the same as 013 with the included stack the other way up, an object over a substitution; the result does not depend on which layer is on top
the included keys stand where the include is, so its two += come first and the file's two append after them (lightbend/config#426)
by default, if an included file does not exist the include statement is silently ignored, so the keys around it parse as if the line were not there
a missing include is treated as if the included file contained only an empty object, so an object whose only content is that include stays an empty object
the silent-ignore default applies to an explicit file() include as well: a file that does not exist contributes nothing and parsing continues
required() only makes the include mandatory; a resource that does resolve is included exactly as an unwrapped include would be
file.conf is a file, not a directory, so there is no file at file.conf/x.conf: the included file does not exist and the include is silently ignored
substitution happens after parsing the whole configuration, so the ${x} fixed up to ${a.x} evaluates to the root's later redefinition 42 rather than the included file's 10
an optional substitution in an included file is looked up at the fixed-up path a.x and at the original path x; with neither defined the field is omitted rather than an error

Settled (Readings): an undefined ${?nope} means common.x.y is never created, so ${x.y} is not found at the fixed-up path and must be looked up at the original path x.y (L1045-1049) — with root x.y = 0, a is 0. typesafe/config treats the vanished value as a miss that ends the lookup (UnresolvedSubstitution), and in some root key orders it even succeeds (see 014): a bug, not HOCON. lightbend/config#863 (open) retries the including root, matching this expect; self-ref/cycle rows 025–028 stay without that fallback.

Settled (Readings): the optional form of 009 — a = ${?x.y} — falls back the same way (L1045-1049): with root x.y = 0, a is 0. typesafe/config leaves a out instead (java: diverges). lightbend/config#863 fixes it to this reading; not the self-ref case (025–028), where falling back would be wrong.
an undefined optional that would override keeps the previous value, so common.x.y is 9 and found at the fixed-up path; the original path is not consulted
the metamorphic twin of 009 without the optional: common.x exists, common.x.y does not, so x.y is looked up at the original path

Settled (Readings): an unrelated key that reads common.x must not change what common.a resolves to — same fallback as 009 (L1045-1049). In typesafe/config 1.4.9 this input fails (UnresolvedSubstitution) while the same input with the observer key named o24bbd resolves to 0: key order decides the result. That is a bug; lightbend/config#863 makes every order give a = 0, as here.
a substitution that is one piece of a concatenation in the included file is fixed up like a bare one: p.x is not set, so the original path x is used
a substitution that is a list element in the included file is fixed up as well
an object merged with a substitution in the included file keeps working after the fix-up, whichever of the two is on top: q is found at p.q
a.x is present, set to null, so the lookup at the fixed-up path succeeds and the original path x is not consulted
as 022 with the object appended by +=: its root is the element, and ${y} finds y = 1 there

Settled (Readings, half b): a self-reference looks back at the fixed-up path only — the original-path fallback is for the application root (L1043-1047), not for a field referring to itself — unlike 009/011/014, where an optional vanishes without a cycle and the root must still be tried. typesafe/config reads it so: a += 2 included at k is k.a = ${?k.a} [2], k.a has no earlier value, and the root's unrelated a = [1] is not looked at: k.a is [2]. lightbend/config#863 keeps a swallowed cycle from falling back to the root, so this row stays as it is.

${y} in child.conf is looked up as b.c.y first, which is not there, then as y from the root (L1010): 1. The path passes b, whose value is being resolved, but it comes from inside that value, not round through another field, so it is no cycle; ${?nope} is undefined and leaves the object

Settled (Readings, half b): a self-reference looks back at the fixed-up path only — unlike 009/011/014 (optional vanishes → still try the root). typesafe/config reads it so: a += 3 included at k looks back at k.a only, which has no earlier value, so the root's text a = "" is not appended to and k.a is [3], no error. lightbend/config#863 keeps a swallowed cycle from falling back to the root, so this row stays as it is.

Settled (Readings, half b): a self-reference looks back at the fixed-up path only — unlike 009/011/014 (optional vanishes → still try the root). typesafe/config reads it so: b = ${?b} included in a has nothing below it at a.b, so it "just disappears silently" (L776), and the root's b {} is not taken: a is {}. lightbend/config#863 keeps a swallowed cycle from falling back to the root, so this row stays as it is.
any amount of whitespace, newlines included, may stand between include and the resource name
whitespace inside the parentheses, outside the quotes, is allowed
an unquoted include at the start of a key is never a key; followed by a separator instead of a quoted name it is an include with an invalid argument
an include stands where a field would, so the usual comma separates it from the field that follows
an include is separated from the field that follows by the usual comma, which only a newline may replace; on one line with neither, b is a stray token after the resource name
the same with a substitution after the object: a { m = 2 } ${x} is a : { m = 2 } ${x}, and the two objects merge; typesafe/config and pyhocon reject the substitution
the [] suffix collects CONFORMANCE_LIST_0, CONFORMANCE_LIST_1, ... until an index is missing, into a list of strings
with no CONFORMANCE_LIST_0 set, an optional ${?X[]} is undefined and the field is not created
indices are collected from 0 until one is missing, so with _0 and _2 set the list holds only the first
an element taken from the environment is a string, so 1 stays "1"
the [] suffix collects environment variables only, so the config key a_0 is not gathered and the optional substitution is undefined
a key is a path expression, built like a value concatenation, so a triple-quoted string can be one, and the fourth quote of its closing run is part of it, giving the key a"
the conversion should be done in a concatenation when a list is expected and an object with numeric keys is found, so the trailing object concatenates onto the array as elements x, y
the conversion should ignore any keys which do not parse as positive integers, so key "foo" is dropped and only "0" contributes to the resulting array

the conversion should sort by the integer value of each key and then build the array; missing indices such as "1" are eliminated rather than left as gaps, so keys "0" and "2" become a two-element array
the conversion ignores any keys which do not parse as positive integers, and "-1" is not a positive integer, so it is dropped and only key "0" contributes

the implicit {} wrap fires only when the file does not begin with a square bracket or curly brace, so a file starting with [ keeps its array root; the include section says so outright -- 'both JSON and HOCON allow arrays as root values in a document' (the reason an included file may not be one). typesafe/config has no array-rooted config at all and rejects the document as LIST rather than object.
an empty array is still an array root, and the wrap rule looks at the opening bracket, not at whether the document has content
a comment is ignored, so the file still begins with a square bracket and the {} wrap does not fire: the root is the array
leading whitespace does not trigger the {} wrap either, for the same reason as a leading comment
foo.bar."hello.world" is a path with three elements: foo, bar, and hello.world, since unquoted dots are path separators but a quoted dot is not
foo followed by quoted "10.0" is an unquoted then a quoted string which concatenate, giving a single-element path
a path element that is an empty string must be quoted; a."".b is a valid three-element path whose middle element is the empty string
an unquoted empty path element is invalid, so a..b must generate an error
a path that starts with a dot is invalid and should generate an error
a path that ends with a dot is invalid and should generate an error
path expressions appear in substitutions as well as keys, and inside quoted strings a dot has no special meaning there either, so ${foo."bar.baz"} looks up key foo then the single key bar.baz
a path expression is always a string, so true in a substitution names the key true rather than a boolean

Settled with the number-like reading (Readings): a key is written as a value is, and 10.0foo is the path 10, 0foo (L496-498). 1e+5.5 is the JSON number 1e+5 then .5, so the path 1e+5, 5. typesafe/config and pyhocon reject the + — the same lenient/forbidden-+ biproduct as path-expressions/024, not a different rule.

the unquoted string include may not begin a path expression in a key: where an object key is expected, include is not read as a key at all and must be followed by a quoted resource name, so include.foo is an error. typesafe/config recognises the keyword only as a bare include token -- include.foo tokenizes as one unquoted string, so it is accepted as the path include.foo, while include = 42 is rejected under the very rule the spec states.
only the unquoted string include that begins a path expression in a key is special: include later in a key (foo.include) and a quoted "include" beginning one are ordinary path elements
if the previous value was not an array, += results in an error just as the long form a = ${?a} [b] would with a non-array a

top.arr += four is top.arr = ${?top.arr} [four], and ${x} { ... } is a merge, so the self-reference looks back at the overridden x.arr, as it does with top : ${x} and top { arr += four } written as two fields; typesafe/config drops the inherited element (lightbend/config#608, fix proposed in #882)
each += looks back through its own concatenation, so y.l appends to x.l and z.l to the resolved y.l; typesafe/config keeps only the last element at each step
the += is three objects down, top.a.b.c = ${?top.a.b.c} [2], and the merge reaches it: the self-reference looks back at x.a.b.c; typesafe/config drops it
the self-reference in b += 2 refers to the b it overrides in the same object, 1, and += onto a value that is not a list is an error, in a list element as anywhere

the error twin of 012: y.l += 2 is y.l = ${?y.l} [2] and looks back at the l = 1 the earlier concatenation merged in, and a number before an array is an error just as in the long form; typesafe/config drops the earlier value and starts a fresh [2]

foo += b is foo = ${?foo} [b], and the previous value is an object with numeric keys; in that concatenation a list is expected, so the object converts to [a] and b is appended rather than += failing on a non-array

a = ${x} resolves to an object, so it merges with the earlier a { c += 1 } instead of hiding it, and the later += looks back at the [1] that one made: [1, 2]; typesafe/config drops the 1 when an object substitution sits between two appends
y's ${?b} leads back to y through b.c's ${y}, so it is nonexistent (L716) and y is [1]; ${y} is required and resolves to that, so b.c is [[1], 2]
as 022 with y written first: y is [1], b.c is [[1], 2]

e's last value reaches e again through c, so it is self-referential and looks back at the first e += ${?c}, whose own ${?c} leads back to e and is nonexistent: c is [] there, and keeps it, as a substitution is resolved once, so e is [[]]. Or c is an alias for the final e, every optional on the cycle nonexistent: [] both (also_valid), as in self-referential-examples/035 and 065. The order the fields resolve in is undefined, so an error is allowed too (L866-881).
as 024 with c written first: c is [], e is [[]], or [] both (also_valid). The order the fields resolve in is undefined, so an error is allowed too (L866-881), as on 024.

a += ${?b} is a = ${?a} [${?b}], b likewise. Resolving a first, b's ${?a} closes the cycle and is missing, so b is [] and a is [[]] (typesafe/config); resolving b first gives the mirror image. Both lists empty comes out of no order: the spec leaves the order two fields resolve in undefined and allows either result or an error (L866-881); a cycle is broken by removing one of its links (L660-661), the optional that closes it, which is then missing (L714-716), and its result is memoized (L884-888). The list form is self-referential-examples/057

026 with b written first. Resolving b first, a's ${?b} closes the cycle and is missing, so a is [] and b is [[]]; resolving a first gives a [[]] and b [] (typesafe/config). Both lists empty comes out of no order: the spec leaves the order two fields resolve in undefined and allows either result or an error (L866-881); a cycle is broken by removing one of its links (L660-661), the optional that closes it, which is then missing (L714-716), and its result is memoized (L884-888)

Resolving c first, d's ${?c} closes the cycle and is missing, so d is 1 next to nothing and c is [d]: the number 1, as substitutions/039 has it. Resolving d first, c's ${?d} is missing, c is [], and d is 1 next to a list, an error (L384-385). c = [] together with d = 1 comes out of no order: the spec leaves the order two fields resolve in undefined and allows either result or an error (L866-881); a cycle is broken by removing one of its links (L660-661), the optional that closes it, which is then missing (L714-716), and its result is memoized (L884-888)

028 with c written first: c [1] and d 1 when c is resolved first, an error when d is. c = [] together with d = 1 comes out of no order: the spec leaves the order two fields resolve in undefined and allows either result or an error (L866-881); a cycle is broken by removing one of its links (L660-661), the optional that closes it, which is then missing (L714-716), and its result is memoized (L884-888)
as 032 with a += ${d} between d and d.z += 5: d.z is [5] and a is [{z: [5]}]
in isolation, with no merges involved, a self-referential field is an error because the substitution cannot be resolved

if the self-referential foo:${foo} comes before foo has any value, the reference is undefined, exactly as if it named a path not found in the document, so it is an error even though foo is given a value afterward
because the self-reference error is treated as undefined rather than an intractable cycle, the optional syntax foo:${?foo} makes the field disappear silently instead of erroring
because there is no inherent cycle here, the substitution must look forward including the field's own later merges, so bar.baz ends up 43 once foo is overridden to 43
an optional self-reference in a value concatenation has to look back to an undefined a, so a ends up "foo" rather than "foofoo"
the spec gives bar:${foo}, foo:${bar} as an example that is not possible to resolve, since neither lazy evaluation nor looking backward breaks the cycle and neither field is optional
a substituted object merges with the earlier object, so its fields are part of the result and ${does-not-exist} is an error
w += 1 is w = ${?w} [1], which reads the earlier list, so ${does-not-exist} is evaluated: an error
a genuine cycle is an error for required substitutions; with the optional syntax it is a missing value, so neither field is created
three objects merged in one value, the last overriding both: ${c.x} looks back at what ${d} ${e} gives c.x, and ${e.z} is an ordinary forward reference; typesafe/config reports a cycle
${bar.foo} is not self-referential, so it looks forward at the final bar.foo, which the object ${r} gives on top: 43, as when the later bar is written out

035 with a defined first: p's last value reaches p again through a, so the cycle is broken by looking back at p = 1, and p = "1x" whichever field is resolved first. a keeps the memoized 1 (expect) or is an alias for the final p (also_valid); an error is not allowed, the cycle can be broken

p's last value is an object, so it is not self-referential and ${a.q} looks forward: a is the merged p, and only its q is needed, which is 1. The same principle as 029, through an alias; there is no cycle to report
r needs v, v.x needs r: a cycle, and a cycle is a missing value for an optional substitution, so v.x is not created. v and r are both {}

${?a} inside a.n leads back to a.n through a, so it is as if it referred to a nonexistent value and a.n is {h: 0}; o is the final a.n, whichever field is resolved first: substitutions are memoized, so both have the same value
${?a} leads back to the field it is in, so it is nonexistent and a.n is not created; o then refers to a path not in the document, an error, not the {} the field never was
${?b} leads back to a.n through b = ${a}, so it is nonexistent and a.n is {h: 0}; b is a, and o is a.n, the same value everywhere. typesafe/config reports b's ${a} as unresolved

Resolving f first, a's ${?f} closes the cycle and is missing, so a is {t: 1} and f is a.t then x, "1x". Resolving a first, f's ${?a.t} closes it, f is "x", and a is the object {t: 1} followed by the text "x", an error (L373-374, L384-385). The order is undefined, so either result or an error is allowed (L866-881). typesafe/config 1.4.9 gives f = "x", a = {t: 1}: it takes a first, then silently drops the text next to the object — the same leniency as string-value-concatenation/010 and 015; lightbend/config#862 (on main) makes that a WrongType, which is the rejected outcome already in also_valid. In 044, the same cycle without the x, it gives f = 1
${?c} leads back to d through c = ${d}, so it is nonexistent and an empty string in the concatenation: d and c are "yes", in either order of the lines
e += ${?c} is e = ${?e} [${?c}]; ${?c} leads back to e through c = ${e}, so it is nonexistent and the element is not added: e and c are []
i = ${d} comes back to i through d.a = ${i.b}, so it is self-referential and looks back: ${i.b} sees i.b = 7. d is {a: 7}, and i is {b: 7} merged with it
p = ${a} comes back to p through a = [${p}], so it looks back at p = 1: a is [1] and p is a, [1], as 035 with the alias in a list
a concatenation with a list in it is a list or an error, never an object, so the object after it does not merge with it and it is hidden: never evaluated, and c is {a: 1}

${nope} [1] is a list or an error whatever ${nope} is, so the object hides it and it is never evaluated ("no matter what ${does-not-exist} resolves to"): no error. A lone ${nope} could be an object, and is evaluated
x's hidden list concatenation is never evaluated, so there is no cycle and k looks forward: x is {b: true}, k is [{b: true}]

unlike 022, the undefined optional sits one level down: it leaves out only bar, while the path w.bar still makes w an object, and that object hides the list, so ${does-not-exist} is never evaluated. typesafe/config evaluates a list hidden by an object that holds a substitution (lightbend/config#865)

b's ${?a} and a's ${?b} lead back to each other. Resolving b first, a's ${?b} closes the cycle and is missing: a is [], b is [[]]; resolving a first gives the mirror image, which is what typesafe/config does. Both lists empty comes out of no order: the spec leaves the order two fields resolve in undefined and allows either result or an error (L866-881); a cycle is broken by removing one of its links (L660-661), the optional that closes it, which is then missing (L714-716), and its result is memoized (L884-888)

Resolving d first, c's ${?d} closes the cycle and is missing, memoized: d is [] and c is no field. Resolving c first, d's ${?c} closes it: d is [] and c is d, [], as typesafe/config gives: the spec leaves the order two fields resolve in undefined and allows either result or an error (L866-881); a cycle is broken by removing one of its links (L660-661), the optional that closes it, which is then missing (L714-716), and its result is memoized (L884-888)

063 with c written first: d [] and no c when d is resolved first, c [] and d [] (typesafe/config) when c is: the spec leaves the order two fields resolve in undefined and allows either result or an error (L866-881); a cycle is broken by removing one of its links (L660-661), the optional that closes it, which is then missing (L714-716), and its result is memoized (L884-888)

e's last value reaches e again through c, so it is self-referential and looks back at e = x${?c}, whose own ${?c} leads back to e and is nonexistent: c is "x" there, and keeps it, as a substitution is resolved once, so e is "xyx". Or c is an alias for the final e, the optionals on the cycle nonexistent: "xy" both (also_valid), as in 035. The order the fields resolve in is undefined, so an error is allowed too (L866-881).
as 065 with c written first: c is "x", e is "xyx", or "xy" both (also_valid). The order the fields resolve in is undefined, so an error is allowed too (L866-881), as on 065.

d.z is written twice, ${?a.k} then += ${?c}. Resolving a walks f, then d, and d.z is reached again from inside a's own look-back (L767): it is still a field with two layers, resolved as one, not a value. ${?a.k} leads back to d.z through a, f and d, so it is nonexistent (L716), ${?c} too, and d.z is []; a is [] with f appended (L731)

b += 1 is b = ${?b} [1], its ${?b} looking back at b's layer below, x${?f} (L767). That look-back is not on the cycle through f, whose ${?b} is the optional that led back to its own field and is nonexistent (L716), so it finds "x", text, and += onto a value that is no list is an error (L731), whichever field is resolved first (071)
070 with f last: b's look-back finds "x" again, and += onto it is an error (L731)
as 070 with b += ${?d}: += appends the list [] even when the element is nonexistent, and appending a list to the text x below is an error (L731, L636). Resolving f first must not drop b's layer below

Resolving f first, e's ${?f.k} closes the cycle and is missing, memoized: e is [y] and f is ${e}, [y]. Resolving e first, f's ${?e} is missing but its ${e} is required and closes the cycle, an error, as typesafe/config reports: the spec leaves the order two fields resolve in undefined and allows either result or an error (L866-881); a cycle is broken by removing one of its links (L660-661), the optional that closes it, which is then missing (L714-716), and its result is memoized (L884-888)

074 with f written first: e [y] and f [y] when f is resolved first, an error (typesafe/config) when e is: the spec leaves the order two fields resolve in undefined and allows either result or an error (L866-881); a cycle is broken by removing one of its links (L660-661), the optional that closes it, which is then missing (L714-716), and its result is memoized (L884-888)
an object with a substitution inside it is not considered self-referential for this purpose, so a:{b:${a}} is an unbreakable cycle that must generate an error
an array with a substitution inside it is not considered self-referential for this purpose, so a:[${a}] is an unbreakable cycle that must generate an error

n.a's ${?b} leads back to n.a through b = ${n.a}, so it is nonexistent (L716), and what is left of n.a is ${n}, a field referring to the object it is in: a cycle no look-back breaks (L688-691, as in 008). typesafe/config gives {} for both
numbers should be kept as they were originally written in the file when they participate in a concatenation, not renormalized
a substitution in a string concatenation becomes text the way a number written there does, as written: 1e5 and 1.50, not 100000.0 and 1.5

a self-reference with no earlier value is undefined "exactly as if the substitution referenced a path not found in the document", and such a path is searched for in the environment, so the field reads the variable of its own name; typesafe/config reports a cycle, which the spec rules out ("undefined" rather than "intractable cycle")

if ${?foo} refers to itself "it's as if it referred to a nonexistent value", and a value not present in the configuration is searched for in the environment, so the field is created from the variable instead of disappearing
worked example: to get a string containing a substitution, use value concatenation with the substitution in the unquoted portion
worked example: quoting the non-substitution portion also forms a value concatenation with the substitution
if a key has been specified more than once, a substitution referring to it always evaluates to its latest-assigned value
a substitution to a key set more than once evaluates to the merged object, not an earlier snapshot
if an undefined ${?foo} substitution is the value of an object field, the field should not be created
if an undefined ${?foo} substitution is an array element, the element should not be added
foo : ${?bar}${?baz} avoids creating the field only if both bar and baz are undefined
the same path with the optional form: undefined, so the field is not created

a path names object fields only, so b.0 does not reach into the list b even though it has an element at index 0; the optional substitution is undefined and a is not created. The list is still unresolved when the lookup happens, which is what makes an implementation look inside it

An undefined ${?x} next to one other value adds nothing: it becomes an empty string only "as part of a value concatenation with another string" (L636-637), "a single value is never converted to a string" (L376), and two undefined optionals make no field at all (L640-642), so what is left is the other value with its type, as typesafe/config reads it: ${?x}42 is the number 42.
the undefined optional creates no field foo, but the path section.foo still made the object section, which stays empty (lightbend/config#615)

An undefined ${?x} next to one other value adds nothing: it becomes an empty string only "as part of a value concatenation with another string" (L636-637), "a single value is never converted to a string" (L376), and two undefined optionals make no field at all (L640-642), so what is left is the other value with its type, as typesafe/config reads it: [${?x}10, 1.50${?x}] is [10, 1.5].

JSON reads only the 0 of 01 as a number, a zero is not followed by digits; what follows is text after the number, as 10.0bar is the number 10.0 then bar (unquoted-strings.9), and a number keeps the text it was written with in a concatenation, so the value is the string "01". typesafe/config reads the number 1. Settled number-like reading in Readings: JSON's number or text as written, not L272-as-error and not typesafe/config's lenient parser.

allowed number formats match JSON, and JSON requires a digit before the decimal point, so -.33 is no number; it holds no forbidden character and its initial characters parse as no number, so it is the unquoted string "-.33", as .33 is (unquoted-strings/018). typesafe/config releases up to 1.4.9 parse it as -0.33; upstream main since lightbend/config#861 (unreleased) reads the string

-.33e+1 has no integer part, so it is no JSON number, and as text it would hold a +, a forbidden character outside the exponent of a number; without the + it is text (032). typesafe/config releases up to 1.4.9 parse it as -3.3; upstream main since lightbend/config#861 (unreleased) rejects it, on the reserved +
JSON requires a digit after the decimal point, so the number is 1 and the dot is text after it: the string "1.". typesafe/config reads it as 1, and lightbend/config#861 leaves it so on purpose
the same with an exponent after the dot: the number is -1 and .e3 is text after it, the string "-1.e3"; typesafe/config reads it as -1000 (named out of scope in lightbend/config#861)

JSON forbids leading zeros after the minus sign as well, so the number is -0 and 033 text after it; a number keeps its text in a concatenation, so the value is the string "-0033". typesafe/config reads it as -33 (named out of scope in lightbend/config#861)
\u must be followed by exactly four hex digits; zzzz are not hex digits
a raw tab is a control character too, so it must be written as \t inside quotes
quoted strings are JSON strings, and JSON's grammar accepts any \uXXXX escape, an unpaired surrogate included, so the string holds that one code unit
number formats match JSON, which has no size limit, so an integer past 2^63 is still a number; typesafe/config makes it a string (lightbend/config#801, ekrich/sconfig#631)
a JSON \u escape is exactly four hex digits, and + is not one; typesafe/config reads +041 as hex 41, A (lightbend/config#884, ekrich/sconfig#623)
a JSON \u escape is four ASCII hex digits; Arabic-Indic digits are not, though typesafe/config parses them as 0041, A (lightbend/config#884, ekrich/sconfig#623)

the same as 010 with an exponent: -.33e1 has no integer part and is no JSON number, and it holds no forbidden character, so it is the string "-.33e1"; with a + in the exponent it is an error (011). typesafe/config releases up to 1.4.9 parse it as -3.3; upstream main since lightbend/config#861 (unreleased) reads the string

number formats are JSON's, where 08080, 01.5 and 0. are no numbers: JSON reads 0, then the rest is text after it, so all three are the strings as written, as 01 is (009). typesafe/config reads 8080, 1.5 and 0; pyhocon 8080 and 1.5
worked example: 10.0bar is the number 10.0 followed by the unquoted string bar, since 10.0 parses as a number at the start
quoted JSON strings may not contain control characters, per the JSON spec, unlike unquoted strings
1+2 begins like a number and is not one; + is a forbidden character, so the token cannot fall back to an unquoted string either
the everyday shape of 025: 127.0 is the number at the start and .0.1 the unquoted string after it; the number keeps the text it was written with, so the address comes out whole
quoted JSON strings may not contain control characters, NUL among them, per the JSON spec

the initial number is what JSON reads, 1e+5 and 1.2e+3 with the + in their exponent, and the rest is text after it, as 10.0bar is the number 10.0 then bar; the + stands inside a number, so no forbidden character is in the text: the strings "1e+5.x", "1.2e+3.x" and "1e+5.5". typesafe/config and pyhocon reject them
JSON reads the number 1e+5, and the second + comes after it, in the text: + is a forbidden character in an unquoted string, so this is an error, where 1e+5.x (033) is text. pyhocon reads a number

-. begins no JSON number, so -.33e+1x is text from its first character, and its + is a forbidden character there: an error, as -.33e+1 is (unchanged-from-json/011). typesafe/config releases up to 1.4.9 read the string; upstream main since lightbend/config#861 (unreleased) rejects it
a nonbreaking space (0x00A0) is a Unicode Zs separator and must be treated as whitespace
vertical tab (0x000B) and form feed (0x000C) are whitespace characters
the spec names figure space (0x2007) and narrow no-break space (0x202F) explicitly among the nonbreaking spaces treated as whitespace
a lone carriage return is whitespace but not a newline, so 1 b concatenates and the second = is a stray token
U+2028 around the separator is whitespace, not part of the key or the value
the file, group, record and unit separators 0x1C-0x1F are whitespace around keys and separators
the ideographic space U+3000 is a Zs space separator and so whitespace, like every member of the category
the BOM is whitespace wherever it appears, not only as a file-start marker
U+0085 (NEL) is a Cc control, neither a Zs/Zl/Zp separator nor one of the listed ASCII controls, so it is not whitespace and stays part of the unquoted key
